card.name: Khiamniungan folk dance
card.tagline: Traditional dances of the Khiamniungan Naga tribe, rooted in festivals and social life.
card.profile: The Khiamniungan folk dances, known as Tsuikuap, are integral to the cultural identity of the Khiamniungan Naga people of Nagaland. These performances range from celebratory harvest festivals and feasts of merit to solemn war rituals and peace treaty receptions. Dancers typically perform in full traditional attire, often carrying weapons such as spears, shields, and the Dao sword. Each dance serves a distinct social or spiritual function, marking the agricultural cycle, honoring the divine, or preparing warriors for combat.
card.insight: In January, during the Khāutsāuhsîe Sümai festival, villagers use stored grain in rituals thanking the Almighty God while dancing beneath snow-clad mountains.

card.profile_long:
The traditional folk dances of the Khiamniungan Naga tribe, collectively known as Tsuikuap, extend far beyond movement and song, serving as a profound expression of cultural identity and historical continuity. Originating within the rugged landscapes of Nagaland and parts of northeastern India, these dances are intricately tied to the rhythm of the agricultural calendar, seasonal festivals, and pivotal community events. Every performance is executed in full traditional attire, notably featuring the Ahangküha, along with combat gear, spears, shields, and the traditional Naga national sword known as the Dao. 

The repertoire of Khiamniungan dances encompasses a wide array of social, ritual, and martial expressions. Among the most prominent is the Langnyu-Khiamjangje dance, performed during the interconnected Miu and Tsoukum festivals. Another major tribal performance is the Jamhang, classified as a Feast of Merit dance that highlights social status and community wealth. For post-harvest celebrations, the Hoi-ie-tsui dance takes place during the Tsoukum festival in October. Social hospitality is equally codified through movement, exemplified by the Shapautaithiu, a traditional welcome dance executed by moving backward while the chief guest follows closely, facing the performance group.

Martial traditions hold a critical place within the Tsuikuap taxonomy. On the eve of battle, a specialized ritual called Kheulak is performed at the anterior of the main Morung by a group of six warriors donning combat armor and weapons. They place their Dao swords on the ground and leap with courage as a solemn vow to defeat their enemies. Similarly, the Shikuoh acts as a fierce war dance where male participants replicate combat scenarios while shouting battle cries to defend the village. The pre-war Tsuichong dance engages able-bodied men in mimicking the aggressive behaviors of roused wild animals such as tigers and bears, utilizing high-pitched yells to psych themselves up for combat. Conversely, the I-li-tsuihang, or victory dance, celebrates successful war raids upon returning to the Morung, renewing the community's resolve to defend their territory.

Peace and gratitude form the thematic bedrock of other vital dances. The Noknap-ie-tsuikuap functions as a peace treaty reception dance, carried out in January when villagers are free from jhum cultivation, marking a mutual agreement to end hostilities and establish peaceful coexistence. In the same month, the Khāutsāuhsîe dance is performed during the Khaozaosie-Hok-Ah festival to express gratitude to Kōuh-ô, the Almighty God, before the new agricultural cycle begins. Accompanied by songs celebrating the arrival of the great Barbet bird and snow-clad mountains, these performances unite the community in shared remembrance, thanksgiving, and cultural preservation.
card.sacred_note: Certain dances like Kheulak and Khāutsāuhsîe involve sacred wartime rituals and expressions of gratitude to the Almighty God (Kōuh-ô) conducted at the Morung.

sections.origins_and_history: The folk dances of the Khiamniungan Naga tribe originate from Nagaland in northeast India. They are deeply rooted in the cultural identity of the people, traditionally marking historical practices such as headhunting raids, peace treaties, agricultural cycles, and communal feasts of merit.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances vary by context, ranging from the backward-moving steps of the Shapautaithiu welcome dance to the vigorous combat leaps of the Kheulak ritual where warriors jump over grounded Dao swords. Pre-war dances involve men mimicking wild animals with high-pitched shouts, while festival dances incorporate communal singing.
sections.music_and_instruments: Musical accompaniment relies primarily on vocal chants, songs, and high-pitched battle cries, reflecting the ceremonial and martial heritage of the community.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers appear fully dressed in traditional attire including the Ahangküha, combat armor, and traditional weapons such as spears, shields, and Dao swords. Settings include the anterior of the main Morung and festival grounds during community celebrations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances are performed during major festivals like Miu, Tsoukum, and Khaozaosie-Hok-Ah, as well as during feasts of merit, peace treaty receptions, pre-war preparations, and post-victory returns.

claims.text: Tsuikuap is the general term for folk dance among the Khiamniungan.
Langnyu-Khiamjangje is performed during the Miu and Tsoukum festivals.
Jamhang is a Feast of Merit dance of the Khiamniungan tribe.
Shapautaithiu is a welcome dance performed moving backward.
Kheulak is a pre-fight ritual dance performed by six warriors at the Morung.
Khāutsāuhsîe dance expresses gratitude to the Almighty God during the festival.
